name: HTML and CSS
title: HTML and CSS: building web pages
intro: Every web page is made of two languages working together. HTML (HyperText Markup Language), invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991 along with the web itself, says what each part of the page is: a heading, a paragraph, a link, a list, a form. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets), added in 1996, says how those parts should look: colours, fonts, spacing and layout. Neither is a programming language in the usual sense, since they describe a page instead of giving steps, but every web developer writes them every day, and JavaScript and PHP pages are built on them. Each example here is a complete page, and the box under it shows the page as a browser draws it. To try one yourself, save it as page.html and open the file in any web browser; change something, save, and reload.

lessons.title: Your first page
lessons.summary: Tags, elements, and the skeleton every page shares.

sections.p: HTML marks up text with tags in angle brackets. Most come in pairs: <p> opens a paragraph and </p> closes it, and everything between is the element's content. <h1> to <h6> are headings from biggest to smallest. The first line says the file is modern HTML, <head> holds facts about the page such as its <title> (shown on the browser tab), and <body> holds what appears on the page. <!-- ... --> is a comment.
sections.code:
Hello, squirrel!

This is my first web page.

It has two paragraphs.
sections.out:
Hello, squirrel!

This is my first web page.

sections.p: The browser treats any run of spaces and line breaks in the HTML as a single space, and it wraps lines to fit the window. So the layout of your HTML file doesn't decide where lines break on the page: elements do. Use separate <p> elements for paragraphs, and <br> for a line break inside one, such as in an address or a poem. <br> has no closing tag, because it has no content.

sections.p: <strong> marks important text (shown bold) and <em> marks emphasis (shown in italics). Extra information goes in attributes inside the opening tag, written name="value". A link is an <a> element whose href attribute gives the address to go to; the text between the tags is what you click.

sections.p: <img> shows a picture from the file or address in src. It has no closing tag. The alt attribute describes the picture in words: screen readers read it aloud to people who can't see the screen, and the browser shows it when the picture can't load, as it can't here because the file doesn't exist. Always write a useful alt.

lessons.title: Page structure and tables
lessons.summary: header, nav, main, section, footer, and tables for data.

sections.p: Modern HTML has elements that say what part of the page something is: <header> for the top, <nav> for the main links, <main> for the page's own content, <section> and <article> to divide it up, and <footer> for the bottom. They look like plain blocks, but screen readers and search engines use them to understand the page. <div> is a block with no meaning, used only for styling.

sections.p: Tables are for data with rows and columns, not for laying out a page. <table> holds rows, <tr>; each row holds cells, <td>, or heading cells, <th>. <caption> gives the table a title.

practice.q: Which element should hold the page's main links?
practice.answer: <nav>
practice.why: nav marks a block of navigation links, which helps screen-reader users jump to it or past it.

practice.q: When should you use a table?
options: For data in rows and columns
To place parts of the page side by side
practice.answer: For data in rows and columns
practice.why: Layout is CSS's job. Tables used for layout confuse screen readers and are hard to change.

lessons.title: Forms
lessons.summary: label, input types, select and button.

sections.p: A <form> collects input. <input> makes a field, and its type decides which kind: text, number, email, checkbox, date and more, each with a suitable keyboard on a phone. Every field needs a <label>, linked by giving the label's for the field's id; clicking the label then focuses the field, and screen readers read it out. required stops the form being sent while the field is empty.

practice.q: Why link a <label> to its <input> with for and id?
options: Clicking the label focuses the field, and screen readers announce it
It sends the label with the form
It is needed for the field to show up
practice.answer: Clicking the label focuses the field, and screen readers announce it
practice.why: The link tells the browser which text names which field.

practice.q: What does the required attribute do?
options: Stops the form being sent while the field is empty
Fills the field with a default
practice.answer: Stops the form being sent while the field is empty
practice.why: The browser checks it before sending and points the user at the empty field.

lessons.title: Styling with CSS
lessons.summary: Rules, selectors, classes, colours and the cascade.

sections.p: CSS is written as rules. Each rule starts with a selector that picks elements, then lists declarations in braces, property: value;. CSS can go in a <style> element in the head, or in a separate file linked with <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> so many pages share it. A selector can be an element name (p), a class with a dot (.warning, matching class="warning"), or an id with a hash (#top).
sections.code:

An ordinary paragraph.
sections.out:
The Drey

sections.p: When several rules set the same property on an element, the most specific selector wins: an id beats a class, and a class beats an element name. Between equally specific rules, the later one wins. Some properties, such as color and font-family, are inherited by the elements inside. display: none removes an element from the page altogether.

lessons.title: Boxes and layout
lessons.summary: The box model, flexbox, grid and fitting small screens.

sections.p: Every element is a box. From the inside out it has its content, padding (space inside the border), a border, and a margin (space outside). box-sizing: border-box makes width include the padding and border, which makes sizes much easier to reason about. Flexbox, display: flex, lays the children of an element out in a row (or a column) and shares the space between them; gap sets the space between items.

sections.p: Grid, display: grid, places children in rows and columns at once. grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) makes three equal columns, where fr is a share of the free space. A media query applies rules only when the screen matches, which is how one page fits both a phone and a desktop: here the grid drops to one column when the window is narrower than 500 pixels. Widen and narrow the preview to see it change.

practice.q: With box-sizing: border-box, a box has width: 200px, padding: 10px and a 2px border. How wide is it on the page?
practice.answer: 200px
practice.why: border-box counts padding and border inside the width. Without it, the box would be 200 + 20 + 4 = 224px wide.

practice.q: What does display: flex on a container do?
options: Lays its children out in a row and shares the space between them
Makes it fill the whole window
practice.answer: Lays its children out in a row and shares the space between them
practice.why: flex-direction can switch the row to a column, and flex on each child sets its share.

lessons.title: Accessibility basics
lessons.summary: Skip links, labels that speak, table scopes and aria.

sections.p: A page should work for people who can't see the screen, use only a keyboard, or zoom the text. Start with a skip link as the first focusable thing: it jumps past the header to the main content. Give the page a language with lang on <html>, put real headings in order, and keep a useful alt on every meaningful image (or alt="" for decoration). aria-label on <nav> names that landmark for screen readers without adding visible text.

sections.p: A control whose visible text is only a symbol needs an accessible name: aria-label on the button, or visually hidden text inside it. In a data table, scope="col" and scope="row" on <th> tell assistive tech which heading belongs to which cell. Prefer real elements (<button>, <a href>) over clickable <div>s — they already keyboard and announce correctly.

lessons.title: Forms in depth
lessons.summary: fieldset, radio groups, textarea, datalist and dates.

sections.p: <fieldset> groups related controls and <legend> names the group — especially useful for a set of radio buttons that share one name. Only one radio in the group can be chosen. <textarea> is for longer text; its starting content goes between the tags (placeholders show only while it is empty). <datalist> offers suggestions for a text field without forcing one of them, and type="date" asks the browser for a date picker when it has one.

sections.p: <details> is a disclosure widget built into HTML: the <summary> is always shown, and the rest opens when you click it. Add open to start it expanded. No JavaScript is required. Closed content is omitted from the page's visible text until it is opened.

sections.p: Pseudo-classes style an element in a state. :hover applies while the pointer is over it; :focus while it is the keyboard (or click) focus — keep a clear outline so keyboard users can see where they are. :target matches the element whose id is in the URL hash after someone follows a link like href="#more". practice.answer: So keyboard users can see which control is active
